lessons.title: Lifestyle and eating in PCOS, beyond weight
lessons.objective: Recommend a healthy lifestyle to every patient with PCOS while distinguishing which outcomes it improves, address weight only if she prioritises it, and do so without stigma or blame.
lessons.closing: Lifestyle for everyone, with co-developed goals; benefits even without weight loss; if the goal is weight loss, a tailored deficit with no unduly restrictive diets; and never blame: there is no consistent evidence that women with PCOS eat or move differently.

lessons.title: Physical activity in PCOS: how much, which kind and what barriers
lessons.objective: Advise physical activity using the guideline amounts for each goal, without imposing an exercise type, and addressing real barriers.
lessons.closing: Some is better than none; less sedentary time; no exercise type has been shown to be superior; amounts depend on the goal; and barriers (body image, fear of failure, safety) are discussed.

lessons.title: Mental health, body image and eating disorders in PCOS
lessons.objective: Screen for depression and anxiety, consider eating disorders whatever the weight, address body image and psychosexual function with permission, and know which treatment to offer.
lessons.closing: Screen everyone for depression (adults and adolescents) and anxiety (adults); think of eating disorders before and during any weight intervention; ask permission to discuss sexuality; and offer psychological therapy when there is a diagnosed disorder, which could be considered first line.

items.title: Healthy lifestyle: for everyone, not just some
items.core: Lifestyle intervention (exercise alone, or multicomponent diet combined with exercise and behavioural strategies) should be recommended for all women with PCOS to improve metabolic health, including central adiposity and lipid profile (evidence-based recommendation, strong; very low certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
A second, strong consensus recommendation broadens the goals: healthy eating and/or physical activity to optimise general health, quality of life, body composition and weight management, meaning maintaining weight, preventing weight gain and/or modest weight loss. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

The practice points add that lifestyle is a core focus of management, that goals and priorities are co-developed with the patient according to her preferences, and that a healthy lifestyle has benefits even without weight loss. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: Who should be offered lifestyle intervention in PCOS, and for which outcomes, according to the 2023 guideline?
items.application: Raise it with every patient, whatever her weight, and first ask what concerns her most (cycles, skin, mood, fertility, energy): that starting point shapes the shared goal.
items.pearl: “For everyone” does not mean “so that everyone loses weight”.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: International PCOS guideline 2023, 3.1.1 (strong, very low certainty), 3.1.2 (consensus, strong) and practice points 3.1.3–3.1.5.

items.title: What lifestyle improves, and what has not been measured
items.core: In the Cochrane review, lifestyle intervention versus minimal intervention may improve the free androgen index, weight and BMI (low-quality evidence), with an uncertain effect on glucose tolerance; no trial assessed live birth, miscarriage or menstrual regularity (as defined in the review). [[ref:lim-2019-cochrane-lifestyle-pcos]]
items.body:
Average effects were small: −1.68 kg of weight and −0.34 kg/m² of BMI. The review included 15 trials with 498 participants, most at high or unclear risk of bias. [[ref:lim-2019-cochrane-lifestyle-pcos]]

The 2023 guideline separates outcomes: the evidence-based recommendation targets metabolic health (central adiposity and lipids), and the consensus one targets general health, quality of life, body composition and weight management. When assessing diet and exercise it distinguishes anthropometric, metabolic, hormonal, reproductive and psychological outcomes. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: Which outcomes did lifestyle improve in the Cochrane PCOS review, and which were never studied?

rows.text: May improve: free androgen index, weight, BMI (low quality)
No studies: live birth, miscarriage, menstrual regularity

visual.alt: Summary of the 2019 Cochrane review: lifestyle may improve the free androgen index, weight and BMI with low-quality evidence; the effect on glucose tolerance is uncertain; there were no studies on live birth, miscarriage or menstrual regularity.

items.application: When you explain the benefits, be specific about the outcome: do not promise that “your period will come back” or “you will get pregnant” as a proven effect of lifestyle.
items.pearl: Absence of studies is not absence of effect, but it is not a promise either.

evidence.label: limited
evidence.note: Cochrane review: low-quality evidence; small trials.

items.title: If she wants to lose weight: a tailored deficit, no unduly restrictive diets
items.core: If the goal is weight loss, a tailored energy deficit could be prescribed, considering her energy requirements, body weight and physical activity level, while avoiding unduly restrictive and nutritionally unbalanced diets (practice points). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
In people with higher weight, weight management can be associated with significant clinical improvements; the guideline asks to consider lifelong prevention of further weight gain, the value of improving central adiposity (waist circumference, waist-hip ratio) or metabolic health, and the need for ongoing assessment and support. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

Changes are tailored to food preferences with a flexible, individual, co-developed approach; barriers (psychological, physical, socioeconomic, sociocultural) are discussed, and referral to suitably trained allied health professionals is considered. Guideline section 3.6 adds that weight-centric care is one option, alongside weight-inclusive care, according to each woman's goals and preferences. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: If a patient with PCOS chooses to lose weight, what criteria does the guideline give for the eating plan, and what should be avoided?
items.application: Before discussing a deficit, confirm that weight loss is her goal (not yours) and ask about previous diets and her relationship with food: eating disorder risk is considered precisely in this context (lesson 3).
items.pearl: The guideline gives no calorie figure and no diet: it gives criteria for tailoring one.
items.deepDive: This module does not repeat the diet content of the pilot module: it covers recommendation 3.3.1 (no superior composition; conditional, very low certainty) and 3.3.2 (consensus, strong). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Practice points 3.1.6, 3.3.3, 3.3.4 and 3.6.4 (group consensus, no certainty rating).

items.title: Behavioural strategies are part of treatment
items.core: Lifestyle interventions could include goal setting, self-monitoring, problem solving, assertiveness training, reinforcing changes and relapse prevention (consensus recommendation, conditional). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
The stated aim is not only weight: it is also a healthy lifestyle and emotional well-being. The practice points suggest SMART goals (specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and timely) and that comprehensive behavioural or cognitive behavioural interventions could be considered to improve support, adherence and maintenance. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

The guideline also notes that lifestyle with structured, intensive and ongoing clinical support appears equally effective in PCOS as in the general population (practice point). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: Which behavioural strategies does the 2023 guideline list for lifestyle interventions in PCOS?
items.application: Communication suggestion: close the visit with a small goal she phrases herself (“what can you see yourself doing this week?”) and a review date, instead of a list of prohibitions.

items.title: Myth: “with PCOS you gain weight because you eat more or exercise less”
items.core: There is a lack of consistent evidence of physiological or behavioural lifestyle differences, related to weight, in women with PCOS compared with women without PCOS (evidence-based recommendation, conditional; very low certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
At the same time, the guideline recognises that, although the specific mechanisms are unclear, many women with PCOS have underlying mechanisms that drive greater longitudinal weight gain and higher BMI, which may underpin greater challenges with weight management (practice point). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

Hence the two messages the guideline attaches to this point: lifelong healthy lifestyle strategies with prevention of excess weight gain, and realistic, tailored goals. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: What does the 2023 guideline say about whether women with PCOS eat or move differently, and about their tendency to gain weight?
items.application: If a patient says “I just have no willpower”, you can respond respectfully that the evidence does not show that women with PCOS eat or move differently, and that in many women with PCOS there are biological mechanisms that make weight harder to manage.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: 3.5.1 conditional, very low certainty; 3.5.2 practice point.

items.title: Talking about weight without stigma: permission, purpose and options
items.core: Many women with PCOS experience weight stigma in healthcare and other settings, and its negative biopsychosocial impact should be recognised (evidence-based recommendation, strong; low certainty). Healthcare professionals should be aware of their own weight biases (consensus, strong). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body: Weight-inclusive practices listed by the guideline (practice point): acknowledge that weight is only one indicator of health and assess broader factors; ask permission to discuss and measure weight, with strategies to minimise discomfort (e.g. blind weighing); avoid “overweight” and “obese/obesity” where stigmatising, with alternatives such as “higher weight”; if weighing, explain how the information will be used; have equipment for all sizes; offer weight-centric or weight-inclusive care according to her goals; and provide best-practice assessment and treatment regardless of weight. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: List at least four weight-inclusive practices proposed by the 2023 guideline for PCOS.
items.application: Possible phrase (communication suggestion): “Is it all right with you if we talk about weight? I ask because it helps me assess your metabolic risk; if you prefer, I can weigh you without you seeing the number.”
items.pearl: The guideline also acknowledges that, with lifestyle change alone, weight may be a non-modifiable risk factor: that does not reduce the care you owe her. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: 3.6.1 strong, low certainty; 3.6.2 consensus, strong; 3.6.4 practice point.

items.title: No exercise type has been shown to be “the PCOS one”
items.core: There is a lack of evidence that any one type or intensity of exercise is better than another for anthropometric, metabolic, hormonal, reproductive or psychological outcomes (evidence-based recommendation, conditional; very low certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
Any physical activity consistent with population guidelines will have health benefits, and within them sustainable activity based on preferences and goals is advised (consensus, strong). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

The guideline defines physical activity broadly: any bodily movement produced by skeletal muscle that requires energy expenditure, including leisure, transport (walking, cycling), work, household chores, games, sport or planned exercise (practice point). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: Is there a preferred exercise type or intensity in PCOS according to the 2023 guideline? What counts as physical activity?
items.application: If she arrives convinced that “only HIIT works” or “only weights”, the guideline does not support that superiority: the best activity is the one she can keep up.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: 3.4.1 conditional, very low certainty; 3.4.2 consensus, strong; 3.4.4 practice point.

items.title: How much activity: it depends on the goal
items.core: In adults aged 18–64, to prevent weight gain and maintain health: a minimum of 150–300 min/week of moderate or 75–150 min/week of vigorous activity (or a combination), plus muscle strengthening on 2 non-consecutive days per week (consensus, strong). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
For greater benefits, including modest weight loss and prevention of weight regain: a minimum of 250 min/week of moderate or 150 min/week of vigorous activity (or a combination), plus strengthening ideally on 2 non-consecutive days. Adolescents: at least 60 min/day of moderate-to-vigorous activity, including muscle- and bone-strengthening activities at least 3 times per week. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

In the same recommendation: all adults should do physical activity, because some is better than none, and limit sedentary time (sitting, screens), since replacing it with activity of any intensity, even light, provides benefits. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: Which weekly activity amounts does the 2023 guideline give for preventing weight gain and for modest weight loss? And for adolescents?

rows.text: Prevent weight gain and maintain health: 150–300 min moderate or 75–150 min vigorous/week + strength 2 days
Modest loss and preventing regain: ≥250 min moderate or ≥150 min vigorous/week + strength 2 days
Always: some is better than none; less sedentary time

visual.alt: Flow by goal in adults aged 18 to 64: to prevent weight gain and maintain health, 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate or 75 to 150 of vigorous activity plus strength two days; for modest weight loss and preventing regain, at least 250 minutes moderate or 150 vigorous plus strength two days; in all cases, some is better than none and sedentary time should be reduced.

items.application: If she is starting from zero, the figures are a horizon, not a condition: start by reducing sitting time and adding whatever is feasible for her.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: 3.4.3 consensus, strong, aligned with population physical activity guidelines.

items.title: Before prescribing exercise, ask what gets in the way
items.core: Barriers and facilitators to physical activity should be discussed: psychological factors (body image concerns, fear of injury, fear of failure, mental health), personal safety, environment, physical limitations, and socioeconomic and sociocultural factors, as well as personal motivators (practice point). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body: The guideline adds considering family engagement and referral to suitably trained allied health professionals. Self-monitoring, including devices that track steps or intensity, could be considered as an adjunct to promote activity and reduce sedentary time (practice point). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: Which psychological barriers to physical activity does the 2023 guideline name in PCOS?
items.application: Possible open question (communication suggestion): “What has made it hard to move more until now?” If embarrassment at the gym comes up, activity need not happen in a gym.
items.pearl: Body image is a barrier named by the guideline, not an excuse.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Practice points 3.4.6 and 3.4.7 (consensus, no certainty rating).

items.title: Screen everyone for depression and anxiety
items.core: Screen for depression in all adults and adolescents with PCOS, and for anxiety in all adults, using regionally validated tools (evidence-based recommendations, strong; high certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
The basis is the high prevalence of moderate to severe depressive and anxiety symptoms in PCOS. If moderate or severe symptoms are detected, further assess, refer appropriately or offer treatment (consensus, strong). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

The optimal interval is not known: a pragmatic approach is screening at diagnosis with repeat screening based on clinical judgement, risk factors, comorbidities and life events, including the perinatal period. Screening covers risk factors, symptoms and risk of self-harm and suicidal intent (practice point). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: Who is screened for depression and anxiety in PCOS, when, and what does screening include?
items.application: In your clinic, build a locally validated questionnaire into the PCOS diagnosis visit and know whom to refer to before you need it.
items.pearl: It is one of the few guideline recommendations with high certainty.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 strong, high certainty; 2.2.3 consensus, strong; 2.2.4 practice point.

items.title: Eating disorders: consider them whatever the weight, especially when weight is discussed
items.core: Eating disorders and disordered eating should be considered in PCOS, regardless of weight, especially in the context of weight management and lifestyle interventions (evidence-based recommendation, conditional; low certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body: If suspected, appropriately qualified practitioners should carry out a full diagnostic interview; if detected, appropriate management and support are offered (practice point). Women with PCOS diagnosed with an eating disorder should be offered psychological therapy guided by general population guidelines and their preferences (consensus, strong). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: In which patients, and at what moment, does the guideline ask to consider eating disorders in PCOS?
items.application: Before proposing an energy deficit, ask about previous diets, binges, compensatory behaviours and relationship with food. If suspicion arises, what is consistent with 2.5.1–2.5.2 (an inference, not the guideline’s literal text) is to complete the diagnostic assessment before proposing a deficit.
items.pearl: A high BMI does not rule out an eating disorder.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: 2.5.1 conditional, low certainty; 2.5.2 practice point; 2.7.1 consensus, strong.

items.title: Body image and psychosexual function: ask with permission
items.core: PCOS features can have a negative impact on body image (evidence-based recommendation, strong; low certainty). Permission should be sought before discussing psychosexual function (consensus, strong). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
A diagnosis of psychosexual dysfunction requires low psychosexual function combined with related distress. The multiple factors that influence it in PCOS could be considered: higher weight, hirsutism, mood disorders, infertility and PCOS medications (consensus, conditional). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

For body image distress, low self-esteem, problems with feminine identity or psychosexual dysfunction, evidence-based treatments such as cognitive behaviour therapy should be offered where appropriate (consensus, strong). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: What does a diagnosis of psychosexual dysfunction require, and which factors influence it in PCOS?
items.application: Communication suggestion: “Some women with PCOS notice it affects how they see themselves or their sex life. Would you like us to talk about that?” Accepting a “no” is also part of permission.
items.pearl: Low function without distress is not dysfunction.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: 2.4.1 strong, low certainty; 2.3.1 consensus, conditional; 2.3.2 and 2.7.2 consensus, strong.

items.title: If there is depression or anxiety: psychological therapy can be first line, and care with weight-gaining drugs
items.core: Psychological therapy could be considered first-line management; antidepressants are considered in adults with clearly documented and persistent disorders or with suicidal symptoms, based on general population guidelines (consensus, conditional). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
Women with PCOS diagnosed with depression, anxiety and/or eating disorders should be offered psychological therapy guided by general population guidelines and their preference (consensus, strong). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

Practice points: lifestyle intervention and other therapies targeting PCOS features (combined oral contraceptives, metformin, laser hair removal) should be considered for their potential to improve psychological symptoms; if drugs are used, avoid inappropriate treatment and limit agents that exacerbate PCOS symptoms, including weight gain; and not managing anxiety and depression may affect adherence to PCOS management. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: What is first-line treatment for depression or anxiety in PCOS, and which pharmacological caution does the guideline add?
items.application: Treating features such as hirsutism (e.g. with laser) can also be part of the mental health plan; coordinate with mental health services rather than choosing one or the other.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: 2.7.1 consensus, strong; 2.8.1 consensus, conditional; 2.8.2 practice point.

items.stem: A 24-year-old patient with PCOS and a BMI in the range considered normal asks whether lifestyle “does anything for her, if she doesn't need to lose weight”. Which answer fits the 2023 guideline?

options.text: Yes: a healthy lifestyle is recommended for everyone and has benefits even without weight loss; in her case the focus is healthy living and preventing excess weight gain.
options.why: Correct: recommendations 3.1.1–3.1.2 and practice points 3.1.5 and 3.1.9.

options.text: No: lifestyle is only indicated in PCOS with higher weight.
options.why: The guideline recommends it for all women with PCOS, whatever their weight.

options.text: Yes, but only if she also loses some weight, because the benefit depends on weight loss.
options.why: The guideline states there are benefits even without weight loss; and in someone without higher weight the focus is not weight loss.

options.text: It only helps if she follows a low-carbohydrate diet.
options.why: The guideline does not support any diet composition over another.

items.explanation: Healthy lifestyle for everyone; in those without higher weight, the goal is health and prevention of excess gain, not weight loss.

items.stem: In the 2019 Cochrane review of lifestyle changes in PCOS, which of these outcomes was NOT assessed by any included trial?

options.text: Free androgen index.
options.why: It was assessed: lifestyle may improve it (low-quality evidence).

options.text: Live birth.
options.why: Correct: no study assessed live birth, miscarriage or menstrual regularity.

options.text: Body weight.
options.why: It was assessed: small average reduction, low-quality evidence.

options.text: Glucose tolerance on OGTT.
options.why: It was assessed, although the effect was uncertain.

items.explanation: Distinguishing outcomes avoids promising reproductive effects that have not been studied in trials of lifestyle versus minimal intervention: no trial measured live birth, miscarriage or menstrual regularity (as defined in the review).

items.stem: A 31-year-old patient with PCOS and higher weight who, after discussion, chooses weight loss as her goal. Which approach is most consistent with the 2023 guideline?

options.text: A standard very-low-calorie diet, the same for all patients with PCOS, for quick results.
options.why: The guideline asks for a deficit tailored to the person and to avoid unduly restrictive diets.

options.text: An energy deficit tailored to her requirements, weight and activity, co-developed around her preferences, with follow-up and after considering disordered eating.
options.why: Correct: practice points 3.1.6 and 3.3.3, and recommendation 2.5.1 on eating disorders in the context of weight management.

options.text: Cut out gluten and dairy, because PCOS is an inflammatory disease.
options.why: The guideline supports no diet composition over another and asks to avoid unduly restrictive and nutritionally unbalanced diets.

options.text: Postpone the metabolic assessment until she has lost weight.
options.why: The guideline asks to offer best-practice assessment and treatment regardless of weight.

items.explanation: If the goal is weight loss, the plan is individual, flexible, free of undue restriction, and attentive to eating disorder risk.

items.stem: Which of these weight practices in a PCOS consultation matches the 2023 guideline?

options.text: Weigh every patient at every visit without asking, because it is clinical data.
options.why: The guideline asks to seek permission to discuss and measure weight.

options.text: Use “obesity” in conversation because it is the most precise term and motivates change.
options.why: The guideline recognises that “overweight” and “obesity” can stigmatise and suggests alternatives such as “higher weight”.

options.text: Ask permission, offer blind weighing and explain how the information will be used.
options.why: Correct: weight-inclusive practices from practice point 3.6.4.

options.text: Avoid any mention of weight, even if she wants to lose it.
options.why: The guideline does not forbid discussing weight: it offers weight-centric or weight-inclusive care according to the woman's goals.

items.explanation: Without stigma does not mean without weight: it means permission, an explained purpose, careful language and options.

items.stem: A resident remarks: “Patients with PCOS gain weight because they eat worse and move less than other women”. What does the 2023 guideline say?

options.text: Correct: studies show higher intake in PCOS.
options.why: The guideline concludes there is no consistent evidence of weight-related lifestyle behaviour differences.

options.text: There is no consistent evidence of weight-related physiological or behavioural differences, although many have underlying mechanisms that drive greater weight gain.
options.why: Correct: recommendation 3.5.1 (conditional, very low certainty) and practice point 3.5.2.

options.text: Weight in PCOS has no relationship with metabolic health.
options.why: The guideline recognises higher weight as a risk factor, albeit as only one indicator among several.

options.text: It is due to a clearly lower resting energy expenditure, proven in PCOS.
options.why: The guideline finds no consistent physiological differences and states that the specific mechanisms are unclear.

items.explanation: Weight difficulty in PCOS is not explained by individual behaviour; blaming the patient has no basis in the evidence.

items.stem: A 35-year-old adult with PCOS wants modest weight loss and to avoid regaining it. What minimum activity amount does the 2023 guideline give for that goal?

options.text: 250 min/week of moderate or 150 min/week of vigorous activity (or a combination), plus strength ideally on 2 non-consecutive days.
options.why: Correct: it is the 3.4.3 amount for modest weight loss and prevention of regain.

options.text: 150–300 min/week moderate or 75–150 vigorous, plus strength 2 days.
options.why: That is the amount for preventing weight gain and maintaining health, not for modest weight loss.

options.text: 60 min/day of moderate-to-vigorous activity, with strength 3 times a week.
options.why: That is the recommendation for adolescents.

options.text: High-intensity interval training only, because it is the most effective in PCOS.
options.why: There is no evidence that one type or intensity is better than another.

items.explanation: The guideline gives two tiers for adults depending on the goal and one for adolescents; in all cases, some is better than none.

items.stem: A patient with PCOS enjoys walking and dancing, but has read that “only weights work for insulin resistance”. What would you tell her, according to the 2023 guideline?

options.text: Switch to strength training only.
options.why: There is no evidence that one exercise type is superior; the guideline includes strength as a complement, not as the only option.

options.text: That walking and dancing count, that no type has been shown to be superior, and that strength can be added two days a week.
options.why: Correct: 3.4.1, 3.4.2 and 3.4.3; sustainable activity based on preferences is what is advised.

options.text: That only planned high-intensity exercise counts.
options.why: The guideline includes transport, household chores, games and light activity that replaces sedentary time.

options.text: That without an insulin measurement the exercise type cannot be decided.
options.why: The guideline advises against routine insulin assays, and exercise type is chosen by preference.

items.explanation: No exercise type is the “right” one for PCOS: choose a sustainable one, within population amounts.

items.stem: Which statement about mental health screening in PCOS reflects the 2023 guideline?

options.text: Depression is only screened for if the patient reports symptoms or has infertility.
options.why: The recommendation is to screen all adults and adolescents with PCOS.

options.text: Depression is screened in all adults and adolescents, and anxiety in all adults, with regionally validated tools.
options.why: Correct: 2.2.1 and 2.2.2, strong recommendations with high certainty.

options.text: The guideline sets mandatory annual screening.
options.why: The optimal interval is not known; screening at diagnosis with repeats based on clinical judgement and life events is proposed.

options.text: Only patients with higher weight are screened.
options.why: The recommendation does not depend on weight.

items.explanation: Universal screening with validated tools, at diagnosis and repeated according to context; it includes self-harm risk.

items.stem: You are about to start a weight management plan with a patient with PCOS and higher weight. What does the 2023 guideline say about eating disorders?

options.text: There is no need to consider them because her weight is high.
options.why: The guideline asks to consider them regardless of weight.

options.text: They should be considered, whatever the weight, especially in the context of weight management; if suspected, a full diagnostic interview by qualified practitioners.
options.why: Correct: 2.5.1 (conditional, low certainty) and practice point 2.5.2.

options.text: They are only considered in adolescents with low weight.
options.why: The recommendation is not limited to an age or weight range.

options.text: If there is disordered eating, the solution is a stricter diet.
options.why: Suspicion calls for specialist assessment and support; the guideline also advises against unduly restrictive diets.

items.explanation: The weight management context is precisely when to think most about eating disorders, including with a high BMI.

items.stem: A patient with PCOS and hirsutism reports, when asked with her permission, low sexual desire, but says it does not worry or distress her. According to the 2023 guideline, what is correct?

options.text: She has psychosexual dysfunction and needs treatment.
options.why: The diagnosis requires low function plus related distress; there is no distress here.

options.text: She does not meet the diagnosis of psychosexual dysfunction, which requires low function with related distress.
options.why: Correct: consensus recommendation 2.3.2.

options.text: Hirsutism does not influence psychosexual function in PCOS.
options.why: The guideline lists hirsutism among the factors that can influence it.

options.text: Sexual function should not be addressed in a PCOS consultation.
options.why: The guideline asks to address it with permission, not to avoid it.

items.explanation: Ask permission, weigh the factors (weight, hirsutism, mood, infertility, medications) and diagnose dysfunction only if there is distress.

items.stem: An adult with PCOS with diagnosed depression, no suicidal symptoms, who prefers to avoid medication if possible. What is most consistent with the 2023 guideline?

options.text: Offer psychological therapy as first line based on population guidelines and her preference, and keep treating the PCOS features that affect her.
options.why: Correct: 2.7.1 (consensus, strong), 2.8.1 (consensus, conditional) and practice point 2.8.2.

options.text: Start an antidepressant immediately, because psychological therapy is not indicated in PCOS.
options.why: The guideline places psychological therapy as a possible first line; antidepressants, in documented and persistent disorders or with suicidal symptoms.

options.text: Do not treat the depression until she loses weight, because it will resolve on its own.
options.why: Leaving it untreated may affect adherence to PCOS management, and making care conditional on weight goes against the guideline.

options.text: Replace the mental health assessment with an inositol supplement.
options.why: The guideline mental health recommendations do not include inositol; a diagnosis calls for offering psychological therapy.

items.explanation: Psychological therapy as first line, drugs used judiciously with caution about weight-gaining agents, and treating PCOS features too.

items.title: Case: Valeria and “I want to lose weight so my period comes back”

steps.text: Valeria (fictional case), 28, PCOS diagnosed two years ago, 45–90-day cycles and acne. She has done several very restrictive diets since adolescence. She says: “I know it's my fault for having no willpower; I want to lose weight so my period comes back”. She mentions that at another clinic she was weighed without being asked and felt judged.

No blame: the 2023 guideline finds no consistent evidence that women with PCOS eat or move differently, and recognises mechanisms that drive weight gain. This is explained to her respectfully before going on.

Weight with permission: she is asked whether she agrees to discuss and measure weight, offered blind weighing, and told what the information will be used for (metabolic risk). Weight-centric and weight-inclusive care options are presented.

Before any weight plan: her repeated restrictive diets mean disordered eating or an eating disorder must be considered, whatever her weight. She reports episodes of loss of control over eating; she is referred for a full diagnostic interview with qualified practitioners (an inference consistent with 2.5.1–2.5.2).
Screening with a regionally validated tool: moderate depressive symptoms, no suicidal ideation. Further assessment, referral or treatment is due; psychological therapy could be first line.

Activity: she feels embarrassed at the gym (a body image barrier named by the guideline). They agree on walking and less sitting time; no exercise type is superior, and some is better than none. If she later chooses weight loss, the reference for modest loss is ≥250 min/week moderate or ≥150 vigorous, plus strength.

Honest expectations: the Cochrane review found no trials measuring menstrual regularity or live birth with lifestyle versus minimal intervention (regularity as defined in the review). For menstrual irregularity and endometrial protection there are specific options; the guideline asks to inform about the increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, without routine screening (1.11.1–1.11.2). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]] Co-developed goals that do not depend only on the scale are set (metabolic health, waist if she agrees, mood, quality of life) and reviewed at follow-up, remembering there are benefits even without weight loss.

items.stem: In the 2023 PCOS guideline, how is the recommendation to offer lifestyle intervention to all women with PCOS to improve metabolic health graded?

options.text: Conditional, moderate certainty.
options.why: It is neither conditional nor moderate certainty.

options.text: Evidence-based, strong, although with very low certainty.
options.why: Correct: recommendation 3.1.1.

options.text: Practice point, with no certainty rating.
options.why: It is an evidence-based recommendation; practice points complement it.

options.text: Strong, high certainty.
options.why: It is strong, but certainty is very low.

items.explanation: A recommendation can be strong even when the certainty of the evidence is very low: strength and certainty are two separate ratings.

items.stem: According to the 2023 PCOS guideline, which outcome does the evidence-based lifestyle recommendation for everyone name, and what does the consensus recommendation add?

options.text: Evidence-based: live birth; consensus: menstrual regularity.
options.why: Neither focuses on reproductive outcomes.

options.text: Evidence-based: weight loss in everyone; consensus: a specific PCOS diet.
options.why: “For everyone” does not mean “so everyone loses weight”, and the guideline supports no specific diet.

options.text: Evidence-based: ovulation; consensus: hirsutism.
options.why: These are not the outcomes named in these recommendations.

options.text: Evidence-based: metabolic health (central adiposity, lipid profile); consensus: general health, quality of life, body composition and weight management.
options.why: Correct: recommendations 3.1.1 and 3.1.2.

items.explanation: Weight management includes maintaining weight, preventing gain and/or modest loss, and lifestyle has benefits even without weight loss.

items.stem: In the 2019 Cochrane review of lifestyle versus minimal intervention in PCOS, how large was the average effect on weight and BMI?

options.text: −1.68 kg of weight and −0.34 kg/m² of BMI, with low-quality evidence.
options.why: Correct: the review included 15 trials with 498 participants, most at high or unclear risk of bias.

options.text: A reduction of about 10% of body weight, with high-quality evidence.
options.why: The average effects were small and the evidence was low quality.

options.text: No effect on weight; only glucose tolerance improved.
options.why: Weight and BMI may improve; the effect on glucose tolerance was uncertain.

options.text: Weight was not analysed; only reproductive outcomes.
options.why: No trial assessed live birth, miscarriage or menstrual regularity; weight was analysed.

items.explanation: Small effects and low-quality evidence: useful for setting realistic expectations with the patient.

items.stem: A patient with PCOS asks whether, with diet and exercise, “her period will become regular”. According to the 2019 Cochrane review, what is most accurate to tell her?

options.text: That yes, it has been shown with high-quality evidence.
options.why: No trial in the review measured menstrual regularity (as defined).

options.text: That lifestyle is useless in PCOS.
options.why: It may improve the free androgen index, weight and BMI (low quality).

options.text: That it was not studied in that review’s trials, so it cannot be promised, though lifestyle may improve other outcomes.
options.why: Correct: no trials on menstrual regularity; possible improvement in free androgen index, weight and BMI.

options.text: That the evidence shows it does not improve menstrual regularity.
options.why: Not having been studied does not show absence of effect.

items.explanation: Absence of studies is not absence of effect, but it is not a promise either: be specific about the outcome.

items.stem: If a patient with PCOS chooses to lose weight, which criteria does the 2023 guideline give for the eating plan?

options.text: A fixed calorie figure, the same for every patient with PCOS.
options.why: The guideline gives no figure: it asks for a deficit tailored to each person.

options.text: A very restrictive diet at the start for quick results.
options.why: The guideline asks to avoid unduly restrictive and unbalanced diets.

options.text: A specific low-carbohydrate pattern, which works best in PCOS.
options.why: The guideline finds no evidence that one composition is superior.

options.text: An energy deficit tailored to her requirements, weight and physical activity, avoiding unduly restrictive or unbalanced diets.
options.why: Correct: 2023 guideline practice points.

items.explanation: The guideline gives no calories and no diet: it gives criteria to individualise, with a flexible, co-developed approach based on her preferences.

items.stem: A patient with PCOS and higher weight who, after some months, has lost little weight but has reduced her waist circumference. According to the 2023 guideline, how do you assess this?

options.text: As an achievement: improving central adiposity or metabolic health has value, with ongoing assessment and support.
options.why: Correct: the guideline asks to consider the value of improving central adiposity (waist, waist-hip ratio) or metabolic health.

options.text: As a failure, because only scale weight counts.
options.why: The guideline values central adiposity and metabolic health, not only weight.

options.text: As a reason to move to a very restrictive diet.
options.why: Unduly restrictive diets should be avoided.

options.text: As a reason to stop follow-up.
options.why: The guideline asks for ongoing assessment and support.

items.explanation: Beyond the scale: preventing further weight gain, improving central adiposity and metabolic health, and sustaining support over time.

items.stem: Which of these sets matches the behavioural strategies the 2023 PCOS guideline proposes including in lifestyle interventions?

options.text: A list of forbidden foods, mandatory daily weighing and a printed diet.
options.why: These are not the strategies the guideline lists.

options.text: Goal setting, self-monitoring, problem solving, assertiveness training, reinforcing changes and relapse prevention.
options.why: Correct: consensus recommendation 3.2.1 (conditional).

options.text: Only written information about PCOS, without follow-up.
options.why: The guideline proposes active strategies and ongoing support.

options.text: Intense calorie restriction reinforced by weekly weigh-ins.
options.why: The guideline avoids unduly restrictive diets and does not propose this as a behavioural strategy.

items.explanation: The aim of these strategies is not only weight: it is also a healthy lifestyle and emotional well-being. The practice points suggest SMART goals.

items.stem: A colleague says: “In PCOS, lifestyle programmes work worse than in the general population; it’s not worth the effort”. What does the 2023 guideline say?

options.text: That he is right: lifestyle is not effective in PCOS.
options.why: The guideline recommends it for everyone and considers it a core focus of management.

options.text: That it only works if combined with drugs.
options.why: The guideline does not make its effectiveness conditional on drugs.

options.text: That with structured, intensive and ongoing clinical support it appears equally effective in PCOS as in the general population.
options.why: Correct: 2023 guideline practice point.

options.text: That it only works in adolescents.
options.why: The guideline does not limit its effectiveness to adolescents.

items.explanation: The key is support: structured, intensive and ongoing; behavioural interventions can also be considered to increase adherence and maintenance.

items.stem: Given the tendency to greater weight gain in many women with PCOS, which two messages does the 2023 guideline attach?

options.text: More intense calorie restriction than in the general population, because they eat more.
options.why: There is no consistent evidence that women with PCOS eat or move differently.

options.text: Rapid weight loss before any other treatment.
options.why: The guideline does not make treatment conditional on weight loss nor propose rapid loss.

options.text: That it is not worth trying, because the mechanisms are biological.
options.why: The guideline proposes lifelong strategies, not fatalism.

options.text: Lifelong healthy lifestyle strategies with prevention of excess weight gain, and realistic, tailored goals.
options.why: Correct: practice point 3.5.2.

items.explanation: Harder does not mean “her fault”: long-term prevention and realistic goals.

items.stem: Which statement reflects the 2023 PCOS guideline on weight in PCOS?

options.text: The specific mechanisms are unclear, but many women with PCOS have underlying mechanisms that drive greater longitudinal weight gain and higher BMI.
options.why: Correct: practice point 3.5.2.

options.text: Weight gain is explained by a lower energy expenditure shown in trials.
options.why: The guideline finds no consistent evidence of weight-related physiological or behavioural differences.

options.text: There is no difference in longitudinal weight gain compared with women without PCOS.
options.why: The guideline recognises that many have greater longitudinal weight gain.

options.text: The mechanisms are fully characterised.
options.why: The guideline says the specific mechanisms are unclear.

items.explanation: Two compatible ideas: no consistent evidence that they eat or move differently, and yet many find weight management harder.

items.stem: What does the 2023 PCOS guideline propose about the terms “overweight” and “obesity” in the consultation?

options.text: Always use them, because they are more precise.
options.why: The guideline asks to avoid them where stigmatising.

options.text: Never talk about weight.
options.why: The guideline proposes discussing weight with permission, not avoiding the topic.

options.text: Avoid them where stigmatising, with alternatives such as “higher weight”.
options.why: Correct: weight-inclusive practice listed by the guideline.

options.text: Replace them with the numerical BMI without explaining anything.
options.why: The guideline asks to explain how weight information will be used.

items.explanation: Weight stigma has a negative biopsychosocial impact (strong recommendation); language is part of care.

items.stem: Which of these is a weight-inclusive practice listed by the 2023 PCOS guideline?

options.text: Postpone hirsutism treatment until she loses weight.
options.why: The guideline asks for best-practice assessment and treatment regardless of weight.

options.text: Having equipment for all body sizes and providing best-practice assessment and treatment regardless of weight.
options.why: Correct: 2023 guideline practice point.

options.text: Weigh at the start of each visit without asking, to avoid discomfort.
options.why: The guideline asks for permission to discuss and measure weight.

options.text: Use weight as the main indicator of health.
options.why: The guideline acknowledges weight is only one indicator of health among others.

items.explanation: In addition, professionals should be aware of their own weight biases (consensus, strong).

items.stem: According to the 2023 PCOS guideline, what counts as physical activity?

options.text: Only planned exercise of at least 30 minutes.
options.why: The definition is broad and includes much more than planned exercise.

options.text: Only gym activity.
options.why: The guideline includes transport, work, household chores, games and sport.

options.text: Only vigorous-intensity activity.
options.why: The definition does not require vigorous intensity.

options.text: Any bodily movement produced by skeletal muscle that requires energy expenditure: leisure, transport, work, household chores, games, sport or planned exercise.
options.why: Correct: practice point 3.4.4.

items.explanation: Walking or cycling to work also counts; the best activity is the one the patient can keep up.

items.stem: What does the 2023 PCOS guideline say about the superiority of one exercise type or intensity?

options.text: High-intensity interval training is superior for metabolic outcomes.
options.why: The guideline finds no evidence that any type or intensity is superior.

options.text: There is a lack of evidence that any type or intensity is better for anthropometric, metabolic, hormonal, reproductive or psychological outcomes (conditional, very low certainty).
options.why: Correct: recommendation 3.4.1.

options.text: Strength training is superior for hormonal outcomes.
options.why: There is no evidence of superiority for any outcome, including hormonal.

options.text: Only vigorous activity brings benefits in PCOS.
options.why: Any activity consistent with population guidelines has benefits.

items.explanation: Any activity consistent with population guidelines has benefits; within them, sustainable activity based on preferences and goals (consensus, strong).

items.stem: A 40-year-old adult with PCOS who wants to prevent weight gain and maintain health. What minimum activity amount does the 2023 guideline give for that goal?

options.text: At least 250 min/week of moderate or 150 of vigorous activity.
options.why: That is the reference for modest weight loss and preventing regain.

options.text: At least 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous activity.
options.why: That is the reference for adolescents.

options.text: 150–300 min/week of moderate or 75–150 of vigorous activity (or a combination), plus muscle strengthening on 2 non-consecutive days.
options.why: Correct: consensus recommendation 3.4.3 for adults aged 18–64.

options.text: Only muscle strengthening 2 days a week, with no aerobic activity.
options.why: Strength is added to aerobic activity, not a substitute for it.

items.explanation: The figures depend on the goal; always, some is better than none and sedentary time should be reduced.

items.stem: A 16-year-old adolescent with PCOS. What physical activity does the 2023 guideline recommend?

options.text: At least 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous activity, including muscle- and bone-strengthening activities at least 3 times a week.
options.why: Correct: consensus recommendation 3.4.3 for adolescents.

options.text: The same figures as adults: 150–300 min/week of moderate activity.
options.why: The guideline gives a specific, daily reference for adolescents.

options.text: Avoid vigorous activity until adulthood.
options.why: The reference includes moderate-to-vigorous activity.

options.text: 30 minutes three days a week is enough.
options.why: This falls well short of the 60 minutes a day reference.

items.explanation: Adolescents: 60 min/day of moderate-to-vigorous activity, plus muscle- and bone-strengthening at least 3 times a week.

items.stem: A patient with PCOS says she does not exercise because she feels embarrassed going to the gym. According to the 2023 guideline, how do you frame it?

options.text: As an excuse: insist on the gym.
options.why: The guideline names body image concerns as a psychological barrier to address.

options.text: Wait until she loses weight before proposing activity.
options.why: Activity has benefits in itself; waiting is not what the guideline proposes.

options.text: Refer to mental health before any physical activity.
options.why: The guideline proposes discussing barriers and facilitators; it does not make activity conditional on prior referral.

options.text: As a body image barrier the guideline names: discuss barriers and facilitators and look for activity that need not be in a gym.
options.why: Correct: practice point on barriers and facilitators, with a broad definition of physical activity.

items.explanation: Ask what has made it hard to move more; body image is a recognised barrier, not an excuse.

items.stem: What does the 2023 PCOS guideline say about devices that track steps or intensity?

options.text: That they are not recommended because they cause obsession.
options.why: The guideline does not advise against them.

options.text: That they are mandatory for every patient.
options.why: The guideline says they could be considered, not that they are mandatory.

options.text: That self-monitoring, including these devices, could be considered as an adjunct to promote activity and reduce sedentary time.
options.why: Correct: 2023 guideline practice point.

options.text: That they are only useful for measuring vigorous activity.
options.why: The guideline mentions them to promote activity and reduce sedentary time in general.

items.explanation: The guideline adds considering family engagement and referral to suitably trained allied health professionals.

items.stem: Of these 2023 PCOS guideline recommendations, which has high certainty?

options.text: Offer lifestyle intervention to everyone to improve metabolic health.
options.why: It is strong, but very low certainty.

options.text: Consider eating disorders whatever the weight.
options.why: It is conditional, low certainty.

options.text: That there is no superior diet composition.
options.why: It is conditional, very low certainty.

options.text: Screen for depression in all adults and adolescents, and for anxiety in all adults, with regionally validated tools.
options.why: Correct: recommendations 2.2.1 and 2.2.2, strong, high certainty.

items.explanation: Mental health screening is one of the few guideline recommendations with high certainty, given the high prevalence of moderate to severe symptoms.

items.stem: According to the 2023 PCOS guideline, when is depression and anxiety screening repeated, and what does it include?

options.text: At diagnosis and then based on clinical judgement, risk factors, comorbidities and life events, including the perinatal period; it covers risk factors, symptoms and risk of self-harm and suicidal intent.
options.why: Correct: practice point 2.2.4; the optimal interval is not known.

options.text: Once a year, at a proven fixed interval.
options.why: The guideline says the optimal interval is not known.

options.text: Only if the patient reports symptoms spontaneously.
options.why: Everyone is screened at diagnosis, without waiting for them to report it.

options.text: Only during pregnancy; it includes mood symptoms only.
options.why: The perinatal period is one of the moments to consider, and screening also covers self-harm and suicidal intent.

items.explanation: If moderate or severe symptoms are detected: further assess, refer or offer treatment (consensus, strong).

items.stem: A patient with PCOS in whom an eating disorder is suspected. According to the 2023 guideline, what is appropriate?

options.text: A full diagnostic interview by appropriately qualified practitioners; if confirmed, psychological therapy guided by general population guidelines and her preferences.
options.why: Correct: practice point 2.5.2 and consensus recommendation 2.7.1.

options.text: Start the calorie deficit anyway and reassess in six months.
options.why: An inference consistent with 2.5.1–2.5.2 (not the guideline's literal text): when an eating disorder is suspected, complete the diagnostic assessment before proposing a deficit.

options.text: Rule it out if BMI is high.
options.why: They should be considered whatever the weight.

options.text: Start an antidepressant as first line.
options.why: The guideline proposes psychological therapy for diagnosed eating disorders.

items.explanation: A high BMI does not rule out an eating disorder; suspicion warrants a full diagnostic assessment.

items.stem: Which statement about the 2023 PCOS guideline recommendation on eating disorders is correct?

options.text: It is strong, high certainty, and applies only at low weight.
options.why: It is conditional, low certainty, and applies whatever the weight.

options.text: It is a practice point that applies only to adolescents.
options.why: It is an evidence-based recommendation and is not limited to adolescents.

options.text: It is conditional, low certainty, and asks to consider them whatever the weight, especially in the context of weight management and lifestyle interventions.
options.why: Correct: recommendation 2.5.1.

options.text: It asks to consider them only if there is amenorrhoea.
options.why: The recommendation is not limited to amenorrhoea.

items.explanation: The key moment is when weight is discussed: before a weight-loss plan, ask about previous diets, binges, compensatory behaviours and relationship with food.

items.stem: According to the 2023 PCOS guideline, which factors could be considered for their influence on psychosexual function in PCOS?

options.text: Only testosterone levels.
options.why: The guideline describes multiple factors, not a single hormone level.

options.text: Higher weight, hirsutism, mood disorders, infertility and PCOS medications.
options.why: Correct: consensus recommendation 2.3.1 (conditional).

options.text: Only age and relationship duration.
options.why: These are not the factors the guideline lists.

options.text: None: psychosexual function is not affected in PCOS.
options.why: The guideline recognises multiple factors influencing it.

items.explanation: Ask permission before discussing psychosexual function (consensus, strong), and remember that a dysfunction diagnosis requires related distress.

items.stem: A patient with PCOS with marked body image distress and low self-esteem. According to the 2023 guideline, what should be offered?

options.text: Lose weight first, which will resolve body image.
options.why: The guideline proposes evidence-based treatments for the distress, not making it conditional on weight.

options.text: Nothing: it is expected in PCOS.
options.why: The guideline asks to offer treatment where appropriate.

options.text: An antidepressant as first line.
options.why: The guideline cites psychological treatments such as cognitive behaviour therapy.

options.text: Evidence-based treatments, such as cognitive behaviour therapy, where appropriate.
options.why: Correct: consensus recommendation 2.7.2 (strong).

items.explanation: PCOS features can negatively affect body image (strong recommendation, low certainty): it is worth asking about, with permission.

items.stem: According to the 2023 PCOS guideline, when are antidepressants considered in adults with PCOS?

options.text: When disorders are clearly documented and persistent, or suicidal symptoms are present, based on general population guidelines.
options.why: Correct: consensus recommendation 2.8.1 (conditional).

options.text: In every patient with a positive screen.
options.why: A positive screen leads to further assessment, referral or treatment; not automatically to antidepressants.

options.text: Never, because they worsen PCOS.
options.why: The guideline considers them in certain situations, with caution about agents that worsen PCOS symptoms.

options.text: Only after metformin fails.
options.why: The guideline does not make antidepressants conditional on metformin.

items.explanation: Psychological therapy could be first line; drugs are reserved for documented, persistent disorders or suicidal symptoms.

items.stem: A woman with PCOS, hirsutism and diagnosed anxiety. According to the practice points of the 2023 guideline, what is correct?

options.text: Treating hirsutism does not affect psychological symptoms; better to leave it for later.
options.why: The guideline asks to consider therapies targeting PCOS features for their potential to improve psychological symptoms.

options.text: Choose the psychotropic only on efficacy, without considering its effect on weight.
options.why: The guideline asks to limit agents that worsen PCOS symptoms, including weight gain.

options.text: Consider therapies for PCOS features (combined oral contraceptives, metformin, laser) for their potential to improve psychological symptoms, and limit drugs that worsen PCOS, including weight gain.
options.why: Correct: practice point 2.8.2.

options.text: Postpone all PCOS treatment until the anxiety resolves.
options.why: The guideline notes that not managing anxiety and depression may affect adherence, not that PCOS care should be postponed.

items.explanation: Coordinate with mental health services rather than choosing one or the other: treating hirsutism can also be part of the mental health plan.

lim-2019-cochrane-lifestyle-pcos.title: Lifestyle changes in women with polycystic ovary syndrome
lim-2019-cochrane-lifestyle-pcos.authors: Lim SS, Hutchison SK, Van Ryswyk E, Norman RJ, Teede HJ, Moran LJ
lim-2019-cochrane-lifestyle-pcos.population: 15 RCTs (498 participants) in women with PCOS comparing lifestyle intervention (diet, exercise, behavioural or combined) with minimal or no intervention; search to March 2018.
lim-2019-cochrane-lifestyle-pcos.finding: Lifestyle intervention may improve the free androgen index (MD −1.11), weight (MD −1.68 kg) and BMI (−0.34 kg/m²), with low-quality evidence; uncertain effect on glucose tolerance. No study assessed live birth, miscarriage or menstrual regularity (as defined in the review).
lim-2019-cochrane-lifestyle-pcos.limitations: Verified against the full abstract (Europe PMC, PMID 30921477); full text not read. Small trials, mostly low quality due to high or unclear risk of bias; high heterogeneity for the free androgen index. 2018 search, predating the 2023 guideline.

teede-2023-pcos-guideline.title: Recommendations From the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.authors: Teede HJ, Tay CT, Laven JJE, et al.; International PCOS Network
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.finding: Graded recommendations (GRADE strength and certainty) on diagnosis (including AMH), glycaemic assessment, psychological management (screening, eating disorders, body image), lifestyle (diet, exercise, behavioural strategies, weight stigma), metformin, inositol and ovulation induction with letrozole.
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.limitations: Many recommendations with low or very low certainty; practice points and consensus recommendations carry no certainty rating.
